मौसम विज्ञान एवं जल विज्ञान केंद्र के अनुसार, पिछले 24 घंटों में शहर के एक बड़े क्षेत्र में लगातार गर्म मौसम और भीषण गर्मी बनी हुई है।
2 सितंबर को, ह्यू स्टेशन पर उच्चतम तापमान 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस तक पहुँच गया, जबकि न्यूनतम आर्द्रता 47% थी; नाम डोंग स्टेशन पर उच्चतम तापमान 36.2 डिग्री सेल्सियस था, जबकि न्यूनतम आर्द्रता 51% थी; और ए लुओई स्टेशन पर उच्चतम तापमान 31.5 डिग्री सेल्सियस था, जबकि न्यूनतम आर्द्रता 61% थी।
अगले 24-48 घंटों के दौरान, 3 से 4 सितंबर तक, एक विस्तृत क्षेत्र में भीषण गर्मी जारी रहेगी। अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहेगा, कुछ क्षेत्रों में यह 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक भी हो सकता है; न्यूनतम दैनिक आर्द्रता 45-55% के बीच रहेगी।
5 सितंबर से ह्यू में तापमान में गिरावट आने लगती है, लू की स्थिति मंद पड़ जाती है और 5 से 7 सितंबर के बीच समाप्त हो जाती है।
मौसम विज्ञान वेधशाला लोगों को सलाह देती है कि वे भीषण गर्मी के दौरान, विशेष रूप से सुबह 11 बजे से शाम 4 बजे के बीच, सीधे गर्मी के संपर्क में आने से बचें; पर्याप्त मात्रा में तरल पदार्थ का सेवन करें और गर्म, शुष्क मौसम के कारण आग, विस्फोट और जंगल की आग के जोखिम को रोकने के लिए बाहर काम करते या यात्रा करते समय स्वास्थ्य सुरक्षा उपाय अपनाएं।

उत्तरी वियतनाम में भीषण गर्मी जारी है और तापमान 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक है।
एसकेडीएस - 3 सितंबर को वियतनाम के उत्तरी क्षेत्र में गर्म मौसम रहा, जहां अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहा और कुछ क्षेत्रों में 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक हो गया।
Báo Sức khỏe và Đời sống•02/09/2026
राष्ट्रीय मौसम विज्ञान एवं जल विज्ञान पूर्वानुमान केंद्र के अनुसार, कल (2 सितंबर) उत्तरी क्षेत्र और थान्ह होआ से दा नांग शहर तक के क्षेत्र तथा क्वांग न्गाई प्रांत के पूर्वी भाग में भीषण गर्मी पड़ी, कुछ क्षेत्रों में तो अत्यधिक गर्मी का प्रकोप रहा। अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस रहा, कुछ स्थानों पर यह 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक था, जैसे: लाओ काई में 38.1 डिग्री, हा जियांग (तुयेन क्वांग) में 37.6 डिग्री, क्वांग न्गाई में 37.1 डिग्री…; सापेक्ष आर्द्रता आमतौर पर 45-50% थी।
3 सितंबर को उत्तरी क्षेत्र में भीषण गर्मी पड़ी, जहां अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहा और कुछ क्षेत्रों में 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक हो गया; न्यूनतम सापेक्ष आर्द्रता आमतौर पर 45-50% थी। थान्ह होआ से दा नांग शहर तक और क्वांग न्गाई प्रांत के पूर्वी भाग में भी भीषण गर्मी रही, कुछ क्षेत्रों में अत्यधिक गर्मी का सामना करना पड़ा, जहां अधिकतम तापमान आमतौर पर 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस के बीच रहा और कुछ क्षेत्रों में 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से भी अधिक हो गया; न्यूनतम सापेक्ष आर्द्रता आमतौर पर 50-55% थी।
4 सितंबर से उत्तरी वियतनाम, थान्ह होआ से दा नांग शहर तक के क्षेत्र और क्वांग न्गाई प्रांत के पूर्वी हिस्से में चल रही लू धीरे-धीरे कम होने लगेगी।
तीव्र गर्मी और कम आर्द्रता के संयुक्त प्रभाव से, बिजली की बढ़ती मांग के कारण आवासीय क्षेत्रों में विस्फोट और आग लगने का खतरा है। इसके अलावा, लंबे समय तक उच्च तापमान के संपर्क में रहने से निर्जलीकरण हो सकता है।
कृपया ध्यान दें कि लू की रिपोर्टों में तापमान का पूर्वानुमान और बाहर का वास्तविक तापमान 2-4 डिग्री या उससे भी अधिक भिन्न हो सकता है, यह अंतर कंक्रीट या डामर जैसी सतहों की स्थिति पर निर्भर करता है।
इस बीच, मध्य और दक्षिणी पहाड़ी क्षेत्रों में आंधी-तूफान आया। कल रात और आज सुबह (3 सितंबर) मध्य पहाड़ी क्षेत्रों में छिटपुट बारिश और आंधी-तूफान आए, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भारी बारिश भी हुई। 2 सितंबर की शाम 7 बजे से 3 सितंबर की सुबह 3 बजे तक कुछ क्षेत्रों में बारिश की मात्रा 60 मिमी से अधिक रही, जैसे कि मांग यांग स्टेशन ( जिया लाई ) पर 64.4 मिमी और फुओक कैट 2-कैट टिएन स्टेशन (लाम डोंग) पर 105 मिमी।
आपको यह भी पसंद आ सकता है
3 सितंबर को, मध्य और दक्षिणी उच्चभूमि में दिन और रात दोनों समय छिटपुट बौछारें और गरज के साथ बारिश हुई, जिसमें 10-30 मिमी तक वर्षा हुई और कुछ स्थानों पर 70 मिमी से अधिक भारी बारिश भी हुई। बवंडर, बिजली, ओले और तेज हवाओं के साथ आई इन बौछारों से कृषि उत्पादन प्रभावित हो सकता है, पेड़ गिर सकते हैं, घरों, परिवहन बुनियादी ढांचे और अन्य सुविधाओं को नुकसान पहुंच सकता है। कुछ स्थानों पर भारी बारिश से छोटी नदियों और नालों में अचानक बाढ़ आ सकती है, ढलानों पर भूस्खलन हो सकता है और निचले इलाकों में जलभराव हो सकता है।
बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और ओलावृष्टि से प्राकृतिक आपदा का खतरा स्तर: स्तर 1। नोट: आंधी-तूफान और बिजली गिरने की वास्तविक समय की चेतावनियाँ; अचानक बाढ़ और भूस्खलन के जोखिम वाले क्षेत्रों की चेतावनियाँ मौसम विज्ञान और जल विज्ञान विभाग की वेबसाइट http://hymetnet.gov.vn/radar/ और https://luquetsatlo.nchmf.gov.vn पर ऑनलाइन उपलब्ध हैं और अचानक बाढ़ और भूस्खलन की चेतावनी देने वाले अलग बुलेटिनों में भी दी जाती हैं।
3 सितंबर को देशभर के सभी क्षेत्रों के लिए मौसम का पूर्वानुमान:
हनोई : न्यूनतम तापमान 25-27 डिग्री सेल्सियस, अधिकतम तापमान 35-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस, कुछ क्षेत्रों में 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक। दिन में बादल छाए रहेंगे, गर्मी और धूप रहेगी, रात में बारिश नहीं होगी। उत्तर-पश्चिम से 2-3 की गति की हवा चलेगी।
उत्तर-पश्चिमी क्षेत्र: न्यूनतम तापमान 22-25 डिग्री सेल्सियस, कुछ स्थानों पर 22 डिग्री से नीचे; अधिकतम तापमान 33-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस, कुछ स्थानों पर 36 डिग्री से ऊपर। दिन में बादल छाए रहेंगे, गर्मी रहेगी और धूप निकलेगी; शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आ सकता है। हल्की हवा चलेगी। गरज के साथ तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली, ओले और तेज हवाओं से सावधान रहें।
पूर्वोत्तर वियतनाम: न्यूनतम तापमान 24-27 डिग्री सेल्सियस, कुछ पहाड़ी क्षेत्रों में 24 डिग्री सेल्सियस से नीचे; अधिकतम तापमान 34-36 डिग्री सेल्सियस, कुछ क्षेत्रों में 36 डिग्री सेल्सियस से ऊपर। दिन में बादल छाए रहेंगे, गर्मी रहेगी और धूप निकलेगी; शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आ सकता है। उत्तर-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवा चलेगी। गरज के साथ तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली, ओले और तेज हवाओं से सावधान रहें।
थान्ह होआ से ह्यू तक: न्यूनतम तापमान 24-27 डिग्री सेल्सियस; अधिकतम तापमान 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस, कुछ क्षेत्रों में 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से अधिक। दिन में बादल छाए रहेंगे, गर्मी और धूप रहेगी, कुछ क्षेत्रों में भीषण गर्मी पड़ सकती है; शाम और रात में छिटपुट बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आ सकता है। पश्चिम से दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा की ओर 2-3 तीव्रता की हवाएं चलेंगी। गरज के साथ तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली, ओले और तेज हवाओं से सावधान रहें।
दक्षिण मध्य तट: न्यूनतम तापमान 25-28 डिग्री सेल्सियस। उत्तरी क्षेत्र: अधिकतम तापमान 35-37 डिग्री सेल्सियस, कुछ स्थानों पर 37 डिग्री सेल्सियस से ऊपर; दक्षिणी क्षेत्र: 32-35 डिग्री सेल्सियस। दिन में बादल छाए रहेंगे, कभी धूप निकलेगी; उत्तर में गर्मी रहेगी, कुछ स्थानों पर भीषण गर्मी का सामना करना पड़ेगा। दोपहर और शाम के बाद कुछ क्षेत्रों में बारिश और गरज के साथ तूफान आ सकता है। दक्षिण-पश्चिम दिशा से 2-3 तीव्रता की हवा चलेगी। गरज के साथ तूफान के दौरान बवंडर, बिजली गिरने और तेज हवाओं से सावधान रहें।

The El Niño weather phenomenon is firmly established and is expected to intensify into a very strong event in the coming months, increasing the risks of floods, droughts and extreme heat across different parts of the world, the World Meteorological Organisation (WMO) said.
According to the latest WMO update, forecasts from its Global Producing Centres show an exceptionally high likelihood of nearly 100% that El Niño will continue through February 2027.
The latest forecast marks the first time a WMO El Niño/La Niña update has expressed such a high level of certainty, reflecting strong agreement among meteorological and climate forecasting centres worldwide.
El Niño is being driven by unusually warm ocean temperatures across the tropical Pacific. The phenomenon is expected to strengthen further over the next several months, reaching very strong intensity and likely peaking toward the end of 2026. Its effects on global climate and weather patterns are expected to continue well into 2027.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres described the developing phenomenon as an exceptionally large El Niño and warned that rising sea surface and global temperatures could put the world at greater risk of extreme weather.
"The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," Guterres said, calling for stronger climate action to protect vulnerable populations.
WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo said El Niño could have severe consequences for communities and economies worldwide, noting that droughts, floods and other disruptions are already being experienced in various regions.
She stressed the need for exceptional preparedness and response as the phenomenon intensifies.
Saulo said the WMO has launched a major mobilisation with National Meteorological and Hydrological Services, describing them as being on the frontline of providing forecasts and early-warning services aimed at protecting lives and livelihoods.
The WMO will also work with UN agencies, humanitarian organisations and other partners to provide climate information needed for disaster preparedness and response, as well as for climate-sensitive sectors including agriculture, health, energy and water management.
"We have no time to lose," Saulo said.
The WMO El Niño/La Niña Updates are considered a key source of information for governments and decision-makers. The forecasts are based on a consensus of climate models from WMO Global Producing Centres, along with assessments from national meteorological and hydrological services and climate prediction centres worldwide.

An estimated 82 percent of the world’s oceans are currently experiencing marine heat waves.
Globally, marine heat waves — prolonged periods of unusually warm water — are becoming more common, more intense, longer lasting, and more widespread, experts say. This year, ocean heat is unusually severe, setting new temperature records. According to Global Climate Risks, a nonprofit created by scientists to publicize the effects of climate change, an estimated 82 percent of the world’s oceans are currently experiencing marine heat waves. Evidence from recent hot spells suggests the impacts on sea life could be profound and long-lasting.
Ocean fevers can rearrange marine ecosystems, drive fish to move into deeper, colder layers of the sea, trigger coral bleaching, and cause widespread marine die-offs. They can increase the severity and number of algal blooms, which harm fish, shellfish, marine mammals, and birds. And they can cause extreme weather events, like tropical storms and hurricanes, and upend fishing and tourism.
To officially be called a heat wave, temperatures must rise above the 90th percentile of normal seasonal variation for five consecutive days. While marine heat waves do occur naturally, climate scientists say anthropogenic warming has exacerbated them. According to NOAA scientists, oceans have absorbed more than 90 percent of the excess heat produced by human-caused global warming. One recent study found that, since 1940, warming has led to a threefold increase in the number of days per year with extreme heat at the ocean surface.
Climate warming and marine heat waves are separate phenomena with different effects. Ocean warming is gradual and allows more time for species to adapt and evolve. Marine heat waves are acute and produce rapid and extreme changes that give organisms little time to adapt. But the long-term warming trend is making ocean heat more severe.
Climate change has raised the temperature of the waters off the U.K. by around 2 degrees F above average in the last six decades, worsening this year’s record heat. Records have fallen elsewhere in Europe as well. “We find it’s the most extreme July marine heat wave conditions for the Western Mediterranean, the Celtic Region, and for the Bay of Biscay and Iberian Peninsula,” said Catherine Gregory, a climate scientist at the University of Bern.
The Pacific has warmed in northern regions by almost 2 degrees F and is currently experiencing the world’s largest marine heat wave, which sprawls over more than 24 million square miles. And in the central and eastern Pacific, things are bound to get worse. This year’s El Niño is expected to be the strongest in living memory — it has already spiked sea temperatures far earlier in the year than expected — and scientists fear it will expand the size and intensity of the two existing marine heat waves off the California coast. Based on studies of past heat waves — in particular, an event known as the Blob, the largest marine heat wave on global record, which dramatically raised temperatures in the eastern Pacific between 2014 and 2016 — scientists are warily watching the warming ocean, anticipating a cascade of severe impacts both onshore and off.
Seabirds in South America have been dying in large numbers, a trend experts say is linked to higher ocean temperatures.
The Blob began to form in the fall of 2013, when a persistent high-pressure ridge greatly reduced the cool winter winds that normally blow over the eastern Pacific. Without that cooling, the sun created a very large body of very warm water. In 2014, ocean temperatures were 7 degrees F above average, and the cold nutrient-rich water that normally coursed along the West Coast disappeared.
The ecological changes were legion. In 2015, researcher Ric Brodeur was monitoring populations of shrimp-like krill, which form the base of the marine food chain, expecting his sampling nets to be full. Instead, they were almost empty. “You could fit all the krill from the trip into a little plastic bag,” he said.
The lack of food caused humpback whale numbers in the North Pacific to drop by an estimated 7,000 — or 20 percent of the population. Many females became emaciated, which reduced calf survival and caused a reproductive decline that didn’t begin to reverse until 2021, five years after the Blob had officially ended.
While many anomalies caused by the unusually warm water were temporary, some were not. The Blob — which at times approached 10 degrees F higher than average — caused large-scale and long-term ecosystem changes, some of which persist to this day. Researchers are concerned that today’s warming waters will compound the damage caused by previous marine heat waves.
One of the most egregious of those earlier changes was the die-off of kelp forests along thousands of miles of coast, from Baja California to as far north as British Columbia. Kelp complexes are some of the most dynamic and biologically productive ecosystems on Earth, the “underwater rainforests” of temperate and Arctic coastal oceans. They offer food, nursery grounds, and shelter from predators and rough currents to hundreds of marine species. Kelp canopies, which consist of rubbery floating fronds, are home to sea otters, seabirds, and juvenile fish, while abalone, sea urchins, lobsters, and octopus live on or near the seafloor.
“The Pacific kelp forest has lasted for millions of years,” said Melissa Carter, a biological oceanographer with UC San Diego’s Scripps Institution of Oceanography, thanks to upwellings of cold water along the coast. “But it has a specific temperature threshold where it falls apart and it can’t survive. And everything that lives on the coast depends on that ecosystem.”
One study found that during the Blob, overall kelp cover dropped considerably: Northern California was hardest hit, with 95 percent of its kelp wiped out. The loss of kelp reshaped the entire food web, decimating red abalone populations, which were already in trouble, and prompting the state of California to extend its ban on recreational fishing of the species at least until April 2036.
One of the largest algal blooms in history now stretches from Southern California to the coast of British Columbia.
The Blob also severely impacted seabirds. Half of Alaska’s common murres — some 4 million birds — starved to death as warmer currents disrupted migrations of anchovies, sardines, and other forage fish. “Recent population abundance estimates since then have found no evidence of recovery,” the authors of a 2024 study of the murres concluded, “suggesting that the heatwave may have led to an ecosystem shift.”
Current marine heat waves are already taking a toll. Dead and dying birds, including California brown pelicans, loons, and grebes, are turning up again on Southern California beaches. “We’re seeing cormorants walk to shore and then just die within the hour,” Tammy Russell, a researcher at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography, told the Associated Press, “and we’re seeing it happening across the whole coast.” Seabirds along South America’s Pacific coast have been dying in large numbers in recent months, and experts have linked the fatalities to higher ocean temperatures.
Researchers are concerned that current record-setting ocean temperatures, intensified by the strengthening El Niño, will further harm corals. Bleaching occurs when rising water temperatures, in addition to other stressors like pollution and overexposure to sunlight, spur corals to release their symbiotic algae, which harvest energy for them. A bleaching event that lasted from early 2023 until mid-2025 affected more than 84 percent of the world’s coral reef areas. In a major report that was just released, Global Coral Reef Monitoring Network researchers warn that coral reefs around the world are seeing a rapid increase in bleaching and that recovery windows between disturbance events are narrowing.
Marine heat waves can affect conditions throughout the water column. When a cap of warm water forms at the ocean’s surface, it prevents vertical mixing and can promote the growth of harmful algal species. The explosion of aquatic organisms depletes oxygen in the water, blocks sunlight, and can release harmful toxins into the air and water.
One of the largest algal blooms in history now stretches from Southern California to the coast of British Columbia. The bloom is dominated by an alga called Pseudo-nitzschia, which multiplies faster and becomes more toxic in warmer water. The alga produces a neurotoxin called domoic acid that is responsible for killing hundreds of California’s sea lions, whales, and porpoises.
It is a perilous moment for the world’s oceans as temperatures hit levels never seen in modern times. And scientists fear the impacts of earlier warming events are only a prologue for what lies ahead.
“The Blob was extreme, the warmest we’ve ever seen anything in 110 years,” said Carter, of Scripps. “We are definitely along the same trend now, and the number of marine heat wave days we’ve [already] seen are exactly on par with 2015. This is a new Blob.”

Extreme Heat Is Becoming an Operating Constraint: SHIRO & Co. Maps the Emerging Market for Usable Human Time
An observation generated through the Kosuke Protocol reframes extreme heat as lost operational time, using Kochi and Tokyo as a measured case.
TOKYO, OTA-KU, JAPAN, September 3, 2026 /EINPresswire.com/ -- SHIRO & Co. has published one of the first applied observations generated through the Kosuke Protocol, its system for turning observed change into structured business and societal questions.
The resulting observation, "Climate Temporal Compression", reframes extreme heat not only as rising temperature, but as lost usable time. It is now being tested through SHIRO & Co.’s Climate Observatory using an experimental comparison of Kochi and Tokyo.
The framework, called "Climate Temporal Compression", starts from a simple premise:
Climate change changes temperature.
But economies operate in time.
As extreme heat reduces the hours in which outdoor work, public activity, recovery and biological production can occur, climate risk may increasingly appear as a scarcity of usable time.
SHIRO & Co. calls this emerging condition Temporal Scarcity.
Explore the press demonstration of Climate Temporal Compression, including the Kochi–Tokyo comparison and experimental usable-time framework:
[PRESS DEMO URL：https://www.shiroand.io/climate-temporal-compression]
FROM CLIMATE EXPOSURE TO OPERATING CAPACITY
Most organizations measure operational capacity through familiar inputs such as workforce, equipment, capital and physical assets.
Climate Observatory introduces another potential variable:
How many of the scheduled hours are actually usable under prevailing climatic conditions?
The Observatory defines Usable Time as the amount of time during which a specific human, biological or economic activity can be performed safely and realistically under prevailing climate conditions.
Its first measured prototype focuses on outdoor labor.
Using hourly estimated WBGT data published by Japan’s Ministry of the Environment, SHIRO & Co. applied the same experimental method to Kochi and Tokyo across 53 complete days between July 1 and August 22, 2026.
The comparison does not rank the cities by temperature. Instead, it examines how the same nominal workday can encounter different patterns of usable time.
ONE NATIONAL CLOCK, DIFFERENT LOCAL OPERATING CAPACITY
Across the 53-day observation period, the experimental model found:
Kochi:
* Median usable-time loss: 1.0 hour
* Maximum usable-time loss: 7.0 hours
* Days with very-high heat constraint: 28
* Days with zero modeled loss: 25
Tokyo:
* Median usable-time loss: 0.0 hours
* Maximum usable-time loss: 7.0 hours
* Days with very-high heat constraint: 19
* Days with zero modeled loss: 34
On July 28, the contrast was particularly visible.
The experimental estimate showed six hours of usable-time loss during the standard outdoor workday in Kochi, while the same model showed zero hours of loss in Tokyo.
The scheduled workday had not changed.
The usable workday had.
SHIRO & Co. describes this emerging difference as Temporal Geography: the idea that operational time itself acquires geography as climate exposure varies between locations.
CLIMATE RISK MAY HIT CAPACITY BEFORE IT HITS ASSETS
Traditional climate-risk discussions often focus on damaged assets, disrupted supply chains or physical infrastructure.
Climate Observatory examines an earlier possibility: climate exposure may begin creating regional differences in execution capacity before physical assets themselves are damaged.
For organizations operating across multiple regions, this could potentially affect project scheduling, workforce allocation, regional capacity planning, automation strategy, remote operations, cooling infrastructure and the economics of maintaining human presence.
This also changes how automation may eventually be evaluated.
The relevant comparison may no longer be only:
Robot cost versus wages.
It may increasingly become:
Automation cost versus the total cost of maintaining safe human presence.
AN OBSERVED ADAPTATION IN JAPANESE PUBLIC WORKS
Kochi Prefecture has introduced a Cool Work Time guideline for construction work that is primarily performed outdoors.
During the summer period, the guideline calls in principle for work to stop between 11:00 and 14:00, with an operating example of 08:00–11:00 and 14:00–17:00.
The guideline recognizes approximately two hours of shortened daily work and allows construction schedules to be extended accordingly.
SHIRO & Co. treats this policy as an observed adaptation and keeps it separate from its experimental climate-derived usable-time estimate.
CLIMATE ADAPTATION MAY BECOME A SCHEDULING PROBLEM
When daytime becomes too hot, activity can move earlier, later or into the night.
But cooler hours are not an unlimited resource.
Outdoor labor may need them. Public life may need them. Human bodies need them for recovery. Agriculture may increasingly depend on narrower viable biological windows.
Climate Observatory calls this potential competition for viable hours Time Competition.
In that scenario, climate adaptation moves beyond cooling equipment and physical infrastructure. It becomes a problem of allocating scarce viable time.
SHIRO & Co. sees potential demand forming around systems that help organizations understand, allocate and protect those hours, including scheduling, workforce orchestration, automation, remote operation and climate-responsive infrastructure.
The Observatory does not claim that these markets have already formed. It is monitoring the conditions under which they could emerge.
TIME AS INFRASTRUCTURE
The broader thesis behind Climate Temporal Compression is that access to climatically viable hours may become an operational resource in its own right.
Clock time is standardized.
Usable time is local.
If this distinction becomes economically material, companies operating across multiple regions may need to understand not only where their assets and workers are located, but when each location remains operationally usable.
SHIRO & Co. calls this emerging perspective Time as Infrastructure.
The Climate Usable Time Assessment is an experimental climate-observation tool. It does not determine legal workability, occupational safety compliance or individual heat risk.

Fuelled by exceptionally warm Pacific waters, the El Niño climate pattern is intensifying and has yet to peak. Forecasters are almost certain it will persist through February 2027 - with unusually warm conditions expected across much of the world in the coming months.
El Niño is strengthening rapidly in the Pacific Ocean, raising the prospect of months of extreme heat, floods, drought, and disruptive weather around the globe.
The phenomenon, already firmly established, is expected to become "very strong" and peak around the end of the year, according to new forecasts from the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) .
The likelihood that El Niño will persist through February 2027 is now close to 100 per cent. Never before has the UN weather agency issued such an unequivocal forecast for El Niño or its cooler counterpart, La Niña .
A supersize problem
And beneath the surface of the tropical Pacific lies another cause for concern. An enormous reservoir of unusually warm water that could continue feeding El Niño in the months ahead.
In some parts of the Pacific, subsurface temperatures in July and early August were more than eight degrees Celsius (around 14 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal.
The combination points toward an unusually powerful climate event unfolding on a planet already significantly warmer because of greenhouse gas emissions.
"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes," UN Secretary-General António Guterres said in a press release on Thursday. "The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up."
El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern that typically develops every two to seven years, when waters in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific become unusually warm. That warming can alter atmospheric circulation thousands of miles away, shifting rainfall and temperature patterns everywhere.
But this El Niño is developing against an unusual backdrop. The oceans are already exceptionally warm, providing a hotter baseline on which the natural climate cycle is playing out.
Scientists have not established that man-made climate change is increasing or intensifying El Niño. But a warmer atmosphere and ocean can amplify some of its consequences, increasing the heat and moisture available to fuel extreme weather.
The latest measurements show how quickly the current event is developing.
The Niño 3.4 index , a closely watched measure of ocean temperatures in the central tropical Pacific, averaged 1.5°C above normal from May through July. By July, it had reached 2°C, and weekly readings from late July through mid-August climbed as high as 2.6 degrees.
The heat extends well below the surface - a sign that the warming is not fleeting and that El Niño has considerable fuel left.
A global pattern, uneven consequences
A very strong El Niño does not mean that every region will experience disasters of the same magnitude.
From September through November, however, forecasters expect above-normal temperatures across nearly the entire Earth's surface.
Rainfall patterns are also taking on the characteristic signature of El Niño, with greater chances of heavy rain and flooding in some places and drought in others.
Other forces could complicate that picture. A positive phase of the Indian Ocean Dipole - another large-scale shift in ocean temperatures - is expected to develop, while the tropical Atlantic is forecast to remain unusually warm.
Those overlapping patterns make it impossible to translate the strength of El Niño into a precise forecast for any individual country. But collectively, the signals point toward a period of heightened risk.
"El Niño means 'little boy' in Spanish, but it has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies around the world," Celeste Saulo, head of WMO , said. "We are already seeing the disruption and devastation caused by droughts and floods, and we expect these impacts to worsen as El Niño intensifies."
Historic mobilisation
The forecast has prompted an unusual response. It's the first time ever WHO has launched a mobilisation of this scale with national weather agencies, seeking to strengthen forecasts and early-warning systems as the risks mount.
The effort is intended to help governments and humanitarian organizations prepare for the effects on particularly vulnerable sectors, including agriculture, public health, energy and water supplies.
"This exceptional El Niño demands exceptional preparedness and response," Ms. Saulo said.
That underscores how much of this El Niño still lies ahead. The phenomenon is already exceptionally strong, and it has yet to peak.
The question is no longer whether El Niño will strengthen, but how much heat - and disruption - it will leave behind.

Taiwan had planned an "extreme heat drill" for government officials and emergency workers to practise their response to 40C temperatures, but Thursday's exercise was almost washed out by heavy rain.
As downpours drenched much of the island, officials in New Taipei City pushed ahead with the first drill of its kind in Taiwan.
Around 300 people from the labour, fire, social welfare and medical sectors took part in various scenarios that were based on temperatures reaching 40C for three consecutive days.
But instead of hats and sunscreen, rain coats and umbrellas were handed out to those involved in the simulations, and portable gazebos set up to protect against the wet weather.
The heavy rain was a "test of our ability to respond and adapt", said Chang Ken-mu, deputy director-general of the environment ministry's Climate Change Administration.
"In the future... we could have extreme heat in the morning and intense rainfall in the afternoon, turning a heat drill into a flood drill. This is very likely to happen in Taiwan," he said.
In one exercise, a man pretending to be homeless and suffering heatstroke lay on the wet ground as two paramedics ran through the rain with an ambulance gurney to administer first aid.
Water trucks with flashing lights simulated attempts to cool street surfaces that had reached 50C by spraying water on the rain-soaked bitumen.
In another exercise, government inspectors pretended to check a construction site where workers gingerly walked through puddles as they moved steel frames from one spot to another.
People simulating heat-related conditions were sent to emergency rooms while elderly people living alone or in nursing homes were also a focus of the drill. Transport disruptions and power outages also featured.
After record heatwaves across Europe this summer, "extreme high temperatures can no longer be treated as just a simple weather event," Deputy Environment Minister Hsieh Yein-rui told reporters.
"They will affect public health, energy, risk, rail infrastructure, transportation, and the ecological environment," Hsieh said.
The large-scale event involving 30 central government agencies, 16 bureaus and departments of New Taipei City, three companies and one medical facility was originally scheduled to be held last week but was postponed due to a typhoon.
"We knew it was going to rain today. The point is... under any conditions, we have to be able to operate," said Chang.
Temperatures in New Taipei City often reached the high 30s during recent summer months, but on Thursday the mercury topped out at 29C, according to the Central Weather Administration (CWA).
Around 44 millimetres (1.7 inches) of rain fell over three hours in the area where the drills were held, which CWA forecaster Wang Pin-hsiang told AFP "isn't really considered particularly heavy rainfall".

BOWLING GREEN, Ky. (WBKO) - When a heat wave rolls in, most people worry about the thermometer climbing and the heat index soaring. But there’s an invisible threat building above our heads: dangerous air quality. Here’s what you need to know about why heat and poor air quality go hand in hand—and what you can do to stay safe.
The Hidden Connection Between Heat and Smog
You might think a heat wave only affects the thermometer, but it’s also creating a hidden problem right above our heads: worse air quality.
Here’s what’s happening. When temperatures soar, the sun’s energy speeds up chemical reactions between pollution in our air—things like exhaust from cars and emissions from power plants. These chemicals mix with natural compounds released by trees and plants during hot weather, and the result is ground-level ozone, or what we commonly call smog.
This isn’t just an unpleasant haze. Smog can cause real breathing problems, including shortness of breath, wheezing, and coughing—especially for children, older adults, and people with asthma or heart conditions.
The Heat Dome Trap: Why Pollution Builds Up
But there’s another critical piece to this puzzle: the heat dome itself.
During a heat dome, a massive area of high pressure settles over a region, creating an invisible lid that traps hot air and pollution close to the ground. With little to no wind to push the air around, pollution just sits there, building up day after day. This stagnant air is the perfect breeding ground for smog formation.
Think of it like this: imagine a lid on a pot of boiling water. The steam (pollution) can’t escape, so it just keeps accumulating. That’s exactly what happens to our air during a heat wave.
Nature’s Contribution: Trees Release More Pollutants
Here’s something many people don’t realize: trees and plants actually contribute to the problem during hot weather.
When temperatures rise, trees and plants release more natural volatile organic compounds (VOCs) into the atmosphere. These compounds react with other pollutants in the air—especially in the presence of intense sunlight—to create even more ground-level ozone. So while we love our trees for shade and oxygen, they’re inadvertently making smog worse during extreme heat.
The Wildfire Wildcard
If conditions get dry enough during a prolonged heat wave, there’s an even bigger threat: wildfires.
Hot and dry conditions increase the risk of wildfires, which release massive amounts of particulate matter and smoke into the atmosphere. Even if we’re not currently in a drought, the drier conditions that come with a heat wave can set the stage for fire danger. Some areas may even implement burn bans to reduce the risk. This smoke can travel hundreds of miles, dramatically worsening air quality across entire regions.
Power Plants Working Overtime
There’s one more factor making this worse: increased energy demand.
During a heat wave, everyone is cranking up their air conditioning to stay cool. This surge in electricity demand means power plants have to work overtime, burning more fuel and pumping out more emissions into the atmosphere. It’s a vicious cycle: the heat makes us use more energy, which creates more pollution, which makes the air quality worse.
Where We Stand Right Now
Our current air quality is in the upper 40s on the Air Quality Index (AQI), which is considered normal and good. However, we still need to stay cautious and use good practices to keep air clean and conditions more tolerable during this heat wave.
Air quality can change quickly, especially as heat intensifies. That’s why it’s important to monitor conditions and know what steps to take if the air quality deteriorates.
How to Protect Yourself During a Heat Wave
Limit outdoor activities during peak heat hours. The worst air quality typically occurs in the afternoon and early evening when the sun is strongest and ozone formation peaks. Try to schedule outdoor activities for early morning or after sunset.
Keep your windows closed. During a heat wave with poor air quality, keeping windows closed helps keep polluted air out of your home. Use air conditioning to stay cool while filtering the air.
Use air purifiers indoors. If you have an air purifier with a HEPA filter, running it can help remove particles and ozone from your indoor air.
Check the AQI before heading outside. Before planning outdoor activities—especially for children, older adults, or anyone with respiratory conditions—check the daily air quality forecast.
Stay hydrated and take breaks. The combination of heat and poor air quality puts extra stress on your body. Drink plenty of water and take frequent breaks in air-conditioned spaces.
Consider masks if air quality is poor. If the AQI reaches unhealthy levels, N95 masks can provide some protection when you’re outside.
The Bottom Line
Heat waves and poor air quality are connected in multiple ways: chemical reactions speed up in the heat, stagnant air traps pollution, plants release more compounds, wildfires become more likely, and our energy use spikes. Understanding these connections helps you take the right steps to protect your health and your family’s health.
Right now, our air quality is still in the good range, but conditions can change. The heat and air quality go hand in hand, and we’re monitoring both closely.

Surprise September heatwave hits Spain: Weather forecast Sept 3-6
Temperatures will climb sharply across Spain on Thursday before the heat finally begins to ease this weekend
Alerts for extremely high temperatures on Friday September 4
Spain is heading into the most intense part of its latest spell of extreme heat, with temperatures expected to reach 42-43°C in parts of the south on Thursday and Friday.
The heat is being driven by a large area of high pressure combined with a mass of very warm, dry air. Dust in the atmosphere will also affect much of mainland Spain and the Balearic Islands.
Meteorologist Samuel Biener of Meteored said the peak of the heat is expected between Thursday and Friday, with temperatures of 42-43°C possible in parts of Extremadura and Andalucia.
He described such temperatures as unusual for September, particularly as meteorological autumn only began on September 1.
Thursday September 3
Temperatures will rise across much of Spain on Thursday, with the biggest increases expected in the north. Galicia and parts of the Cantabrian coast could see temperatures climb by as much as four to eight degrees in just 24 hours.
Despite the sharp rise in the north, the hottest conditions will remain further south. Temperatures could reach 42-43°C around the Guadiana and Guadalquivir valleys, while much of inland Spain will exceed 35°C.
The Ebro Valley and parts of northeastern Spain could reach around 37°C, while temperatures are expected to pass 34°C across large areas of the northern plateau.
Friday September 4
The extreme heat will continue on Friday and could spread to more parts of the country. Badajoz, Córdoba and Seville could again reach 42-43°C, while Zaragoza, Lleida, Ciudad Real, Toledo and Cáceres could see temperatures rise above 40°C.
The nights will also remain exceptionally warm. Minimum temperatures could stay at 25°C or higher in parts of Andalucia, along the Mediterranean coast, the Balearic Islands and the Canary Islands.
The Canary Islands will also remain hot, with some mid-altitude areas of Gran Canaria reaching 35°C or more.
Saturday September 5
Temperatures should begin to fall in the south and northwest on Saturday, although it will remain warmer than normal for early September.
Cloudier conditions are expected in western Spain, with showers and thunderstorms possible in the northwest and potentially extending into parts of the southwest.
Sunday September 6
The gradual change to cooler conditions will continue on Sunday, particularly in the northwest. Galicia, Asturias and Cantabria could see a significant drop in temperatures, while other areas will see smaller falls.
The east and the Balearic Islands will remain comparatively warm, although temperatures should begin moving back towards more normal levels.
There is still some uncertainty over how quickly the cooler Atlantic air will spread across Spain, with the weather pattern potentially bringing further instability and thunderstorms over the weekend.
Forecasters have warned that temperatures could rise again next week, meaning the unusual September heat may not be over just yet.
According to Mr Biener, this episode could even last long enough to meet the criteria for a heatwave.
"We're facing an episode that 's borderline being considered a heat wave due to its duration; we'll have to see if it ultimately becomes one," he explained.

A strong monsoon system is likely to bring heavy rain to several parts of Madhya Pradesh on Thursday. Narmadapuram and Chhindwara are under a red alert for extremely heavy rain, while six districts — Chhatarpur, Sagar, Raisen, Narsinghpur, Seoni and Betul — are under an orange alert.
More than 4 inches of rain could fall in these districts over the next 24 hours.
According to the weather department, heavy rain is also likely in Sehore, Agar-Malwa, Rajgarh, Guna, Vidisha, Ashoknagar, Shivpuri, Datia, Niwari, Tikamgarh, Damoh, Panna, Satna, Maihar, Katni, Jabalpur, Dindori, Mandla, Pandhurna and Balaghat.
Bhopal, Raisen, Indore, Dhar, Alirajpur, Burhanpur, Barwani, Khandwa, Khargone, Jhabua, Ujjain, Neemuch, Mandsaur, Shajapur, Dewas, Ratlam, Betul, Harda, Gwalior, Morena, Bhind, Sheopur, Seoni, Narsinghpur, Rewa, Sidhi, Singrauli, Mauganj, Shahdol, Umaria, Anuppur, Sagar and Chhatarpur may receive rain ranging from light to heavy.
System to affect western MP from Friday
Weather experts said the system will move further on September 4, with its impact expected to be stronger across the Bhopal, Ujjain, Gwalior, Sagar, Narmadapuram and Chambal divisions.
Heavy rain is possible in Bhopal, Ujjain and Gwalior, while no significant heavy rain is expected in Indore.
The northern parts of the state may receive heavy rain on September 5. On September 6, the system is expected to remain active over the Gwalior-Chambal division.
Water levels rising in dams
Continuous rainfall has improved the water levels in dams across the state. Most reservoirs have reached around 70% of their capacity, and gates of some dams have already been opened.
However, the situation remains less favourable in the Indore and Ujjain divisions.
The water level in Bhopal's Upper Lake has reached 1,666.50 feet, leaving just 0.30 feet of capacity. Once the lake reaches full capacity, the gates of Bhadbhada Dam will be opened.
Water released from Bhadbhada will flow into the Kaliyasot Dam, causing its water level to rise as well.
MP records 28.1 inches of rain so far
According to the weather department, Madhya Pradesh has received 714.2 mm (28.1 inches) of rain so far this monsoon.
The state normally receives 799.9 mm (31.5 inches) by this point, meaning rainfall is currently 3.4 inches below normal. Overall, the state has received 11% less rain than normal.
Rainfall is 4% below normal in eastern MP and 17% below normal in the western part of the state.
Photos of the rain on Wednesday
40 districts record rainfall deficit
In eastern Madhya Pradesh, covering the Jabalpur, Rewa, Sagar and Shahdol divisions, rainfall is up to 17% below normal.
Several districts, including Balaghat, Chhatarpur, Dindori, Chhindwara, Damoh, Jabalpur, Katni, Maihar, Mandla, Narsinghpur, Niwari, Pandhurna, Panna, Rewa, Sagar, Seoni and Tikamgarh, have recorded rainfall deficits ranging from 2% to 51%.
In western MP, Agar-Malwa, Alirajpur, Ashoknagar, Betul, Datia, Dewas, Dhar, Harda, Indore, Jhabua, Morena, Mandsaur, Narmadapuram, Neemuch, Barwani, Khandwa, Raisen, Ratlam, Sehore, Shajapur, Sheopur, Shivpuri, Ujjain and Vidisha have recorded 2% to 53% less rainfall than normal.
16 districts receive above-normal rainfall
Sixteen districts have received more rainfall than normal so far. These include Anuppur, Mauganj, Niwari, Satna, Shahdol, Sidhi, Singrauli, Umaria, Bhind, Bhopal, Burhanpur, Guna, Gwalior, Khargone, Rajgarh and Shivpuri.
July and August improve rainfall after weak June
Madhya Pradesh received 14% less rainfall than normal in June. Heavy rain during the early days of July helped improve the figures.
The monsoon then went into a break twice, resulting in several dry days. A strong system became active again during the final week.
Despite this, rainfall remains 13% below normal for the period mentioned by the weather department. July and August have received their expected rainfall, but the June deficit has not been fully recovered.
This has left the state's overall rainfall 11% below normal so far.
Madhya Pradesh's normal annual rainfall is 37.3 inches. Bhopal, Indore, Jabalpur and Gwalior each receive around 38-39 inches of rain on average.
Rainfall records in five major MP cities
Bhopal: Above-normal rain for four years
Bhopal normally receives around 7 inches of rain in September, but the city has recorded above-normal rainfall for the past five years.
The overall September record was set in 1961, when more than 30 inches of rain was recorded during the month. The highest 24-hour rainfall — 9.2 inches — was recorded on September 2, 1947.
Bhopal receives rain on an average of 8-10 days in September. The average maximum temperature is around 31.3°C, while the minimum is around 22.2°C.
Indore: September record stands at 30 inches
Indore's September rainfall record stands at around 30 inches, recorded in 1954.
The city received nearly 6.75 inches of rain in 24 hours on September 20, 1987.
Indore receives rainfall on an average of eight days during September.
Gwalior: 25.5 inches recorded in September 1990
Gwalior received 647 mm (25.5 inches) of rain in September 1990, its highest monthly September rainfall on record.
The city recorded 12.5 inches of rain in 24 hours on September 7, 1988.
Gwalior normally receives around 6 inches of rain in September, but rainfall has remained above normal for the past four years.
The city's August rainfall quota was already completed this year, so any rain received in September will effectively be additional rainfall.
Jabalpur: 8.5-inch 24-hour rainfall record
Jabalpur also receives significant rainfall during September. The city recorded 8.5 inches of rain within 24 hours on September 20, 1926.
Its highest monthly September rainfall was also recorded in 1926, when the city received around 32 inches.
Jabalpur receives rain on an average of 10 days in September, with normal monthly rainfall of around 8.5 inches. The city has recorded above-normal rainfall for the past three years.
Ujjain: September rainfall once filled the entire monsoon quota
Ujjain's normal annual rainfall is 34.81 inches. In 1961, rainfall during September alone was enough to take the city past its normal full-season rainfall.
The city received 1,089 mm (around 43 inches) in September that year. Its highest 24-hour rainfall record is around 5.5 inches, recorded on September 27, 1961.
Ujjain normally receives around 6.75 inches of rain in September, but rainfall has exceeded 12 inches in each of the past two years. The city receives rain on an average of seven days during the month.

search_term: ("heat advisory" OR "heat action plan" OR "heat alert" OR "IMD warning" OR "IMD alert" OR "red alert" OR "orange alert" OR "yellow alert" OR "NDMA advisory" OR "cooling shelter" OR "relief measures" OR "heat compensation" OR "severe weather warning") Andaman and Nicobar Islands
full_text:
A month ago, the alert status of the Purace volcano changed from yellow to orange. The volcanic chain of which it is part, Los Coconucos, in the department of Cauca, remains active and keeps the country in a state of constant expectation.
For this reason, the Colombian Geological Service (SGC) once again referred to the hazard map, a tool containing the keys to risk management based on scientific information.
The SGC recalls that the Purace volcano is located in the department of Cauca, 27 kilometers southeast of Popayan, and has a monitoring network made up of 121 stations, 71 of them telemetric, and around 50 sampling points for gases, hot springs and deformation measurements, among others.
The latest version of the Purace volcano hazard map, prepared by SGC scientists, dates from 2014 and has been shared with departmental, municipal and Indigenous authorities, especially the councils of Purace, Paletara and Coconuco, since the area of high and medium hazard influence is mainly Indigenous and peasant.
The map establishes that there are three hazard zones in the event of an eruption of the Purace volcano: high (red), medium (orange) and low (yellow). The boundaries between the three are transitional because volcanic phenomena do not behave uniformly, which is why they are represented with dashed lines.
High hazard zone
It comprises the area closest to the crater, part of the municipalities of Popayan and Purace, especially their rural districts of Campamento, Pululo, Alto Anambio, Chapio, Tabio, Hispala, Cristal, Chiliglo, Patugo and Cobalo. It also includes the basins of the Cocuy, San Francisco, Vinagre and Anambio rivers, and the Agua Blanca creek, among other tributaries of the Cauca River.
In this high hazard zone, during an eruption of the Purace volcano, phenomena such as the fall of pyroclasts and pyroclastic density currents could occur (a mixture of hot gases, ash and rocks that could descend at hundreds of kilometers per hour down the slopes of the volcano), traveling distances of around 10 km from the emission source.
In the same high hazard zone, mudflows could also occur, traveling through the valleys of rivers and streams that originate at the volcano; lava flows that would affect the highest parts of the volcano; bombs and blocks emitted as ballistic projectiles (fragments expelled from the volcano at high speed) with diameters of centimeters or even meters, which may be solid (blocks) or fragments of molten rock that cool upon contact with the air (bombs). Shock waves and earthquakes that could be felt could also occur.
Medium and low hazard zones
But things change in the medium hazard zone, where rural districts such as Hispala and Hato Viejo (in the municipality of Purace); Alto Pasares (in Popayan) and rural districts of the municipality of Timbio, among others, are located.
There, phenomena such as the fall of pyroclasts with accumulations between 10 mm and 1 cm could occur; ballistic projectiles with diameters between 6 and 20 cm; shock waves generated by explosive eruptions, and earthquakes that could be felt.
The low hazard zone includes part of the municipalities of Popayan, Purace, Totoro and El Tambo, among others. In these places, ash could fall with accumulations of 1 cm to 5 mm; as well as seismic activity and shock waves due to the explosive activity of the volcano.
To prepare this map, SGC experts analyzed the eruptive history of the Purace volcano over the last 10,000 years, and currently are integrating the hazard map of the Purace, Curiquinga and Piocollo volcanoes, which are part of the Los Coconucos volcanic chain.
Based on this knowledge, strategies can be developed for proper risk management, the response of different local, departmental and national authorities can be prepared, and territorial planning policies can be guided to preserve the lives of inhabitants living in volcanic influence zones.
The volcano may experience temporary variations
The SGC, through the Popayan Volcanological and Seismological Observatory, monitors this Purace volcano 24/7 and promptly reports any change in its status through its website, social media and permanent communication with local, regional and national authorities.
According to the SGC’s most recent report, several of the monitored parameters have reached some of the highest levels recorded during recent weeks, which is why authorities maintain permanent surveillance of the volcano’s evolution.
“A predominance of seismic signals associated with fluid dynamics in the volcanic conduits remains on record, especially tremor-type signals (TR), which continue to be located beneath the crater of the Purace volcano at depths of less than 1 km,” stated the latest communiqué issued by the agency.
In recent reports, around 80 earthquakes were recorded, located between 10 and 15 kilometers northeast of the volcano, with depths ranging between 7 and 11 kilometers. In addition, a slow process of ground deformation persists in the area between the Purace, Piocollo and Curiquinga volcanoes.
The SGC stated that the volcano’s activity may experience temporary variations, meaning that at certain times it could decrease compared with the levels observed in previous days or weeks. But a temporary reduction does not necessarily mean that Purace has returned to a stable state, so monitoring is maintained for any change in its behavior.
The SGC recommends that the community avoid approaching the craters of the Purace, Piocollo and Curiquinga volcanoes, as well as the headwaters of the rivers that originate in these areas. The agency warned that sudden emissions of gases and ash may occur there, in addition to the ejection of rock fragments, and therefore urged people to maintain precautionary measures.

title: Love for shoes, purses and jewelry linked to fertility - kake.com

full_text:
By Stephen Beech
Women's love for bling may be driven by fertility, according to a new study.
Researchers found that they show a "stronger desire" to buy "conspicuous luxury goods" — such as designer handbags, shoes and jewelry — during ovulation when they are most fertile.
Scientists say their findings suggest that a woman's drive to wear expensive status symbols — potentially to be noticed by men — is linked to hormonal fluctuations.
Study leader Aekyoung Kim said: "Consumers spend billions of dollars each year on high-end goods such as designer clothes and accessories, jewelry, and luxury cars, often to signal wealth and prestige.
"Women account for nearly half of the spending on luxury goods and services, in part to communicate their status."
Kim and her colleagues at Jeonbuk National University in Jeonju, South Korea, looked at whether, beyond seeking status, women display luxury goods to attract partners near ovulation, when estrogen levels increase and fertility is high.
The research team predicted that women near ovulation are more likely to prefer designer bags and shoes and display luxury in a conspicuous way, such as by wearing clothes with large logos that others will notice.
To investigate, they conducted a series of studies using urine samples to measure hormone levels and a survey method that estimated a woman's current phase in the menstrual cycle.
In the first, 70 female university students who were not on hormonal contraception were asked to draw logos of luxury brands — such as Gucci, Chanel and Louis Vuitton.
The participants drew larger logos near ovulation compared with the low-fertility phase of the cycle, supporting the idea that women prefer more conspicuous luxury during that time to help them be noticed by men.
In the second, 1,486 women who were not taking hormonal contraceptives were asked about their buying intentions for luxury and non-luxury brands.
The results showed that ovulating women have an increased desire to buy luxury consumed in public, but not in private.
Kim says that indicates that the increased desire for luxury near ovulation occurs because conspicuous luxury may increase the chance that women will be noticed.
The third study, involving 966 participants, showed that women near ovulation were more likely to choose a $100 gift certificate from a luxury brand — such as Polo Ralph Lauren — over a non-luxury brand.
But when they read about research findings showing that men don't notice women's designer clothes, they were less likely to choose a luxury brand, even when they were near ovulation.
Kim said the results, published in the journal PLOS One, provide further evidence that women who are near ovulation use conspicuous luxury consumption to be noticed by men.
She pointed out that the experiments were not designed to produce causal evidence, and the findings don't apply to every context in which women attempt to attract men.
But, despite those limitations, Kim said the overall evidence provides support for the idea that women's ovulatory cycle can influence their behavior toward men, especially with regard to using bling to be noticed.
She added: "What we found most interesting is that the effect of ovulation on luxury desire is not simply a general increase in preference for expensive products.
"Rather, it appears to be socially strategic: the effect becomes stronger when luxury consumption is visible and personally relevant but disappears when women believe that men do not pay attention to such signals."

Visayas, Mindanao grids remain under red alert Thursday
MANILA, Philippines – The unavailability of several power plants in the Visayas and Mindanao continues to trigger red and yellow alerts Thursday as electricity demand remains high.
In an advisory, the National Grid Corp. of the Philippines (NGCP) said the Visayas grid will be under red alert for nine hours, from 1 p.m. to 10 p.m., while yellow alerts will be in effect from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. and 10 p.m. to 11 p.m.
Available capacity stands at about 2,187 megawatts (MW), while peak demand is expected to reach 2,575 MW.
Unit 1 of Therma Visayas Inc. and Unit 3 of Panay Energy Development Corp. remain on forced outage, along with four other units that have been unavailable this month.
NGCP said more than 20 other units have been unavailable since 2021, while 16 power plants are operating at derated capacities, resulting in a total capacity loss of about 792 MW.
Electricity imports from the Mindanao grid are also low, further limiting available capacity in the Visayas, it said.
In Mindanao, available capacity is about 2,480 MW, below the combined requirements for peak demand, contingency and regulating reserves. Peak demand is expected to reach 2,546 MW.
The Mindanao grid will be under red alert for nine hours, from noon to 9 p.m., and yellow alert from 10 a.m. to noon and 9 p.m. to 10 p.m.
NGCP said six power plants are on forced outage this month, primarily Units 1 and 2 of GNPower Kauswagan and Unit 2 of Therma South Inc.
Four other power plants have been unavailable this month, while 21 others have been on forced outage since early 2024.
Seven additional plants are operating at derated capacities, bringing the total capacity loss to about 841.6 MW.
NGCP issues a yellow alert when available capacity falls below a grid’s contingency requirement. A red alert is issued when available capacity is insufficient to meet both demand and the grid’s contingency requirement. (PNA)

full_text:
Temperatures of 40C or higher are set to hit parts of mainland Spain as the country swelters in a fresh heatwave.
The heatwave began on Wednesday and is expected to last until Friday, with Spain's state weather service AEMET issuing orange weather alerts across large parts of the country, particularly in the south. The alerts, in place from 1pm until 8.59pm local time on both Thursday and Friday, warn that weather conditions pose an "important hazard".
Spain's Civil Protection service issued a warning on Tuesday over "very high and persistent temperatures" expected to last until Friday. It said the risk of wildfires would rise again to "extreme levels", with possible dry afternoon storms adding to the danger. Wildfires have burned through more than 295,000 hectares in Spain so far this year.
Thursday is expected to be the hottest day, with temperatures soaring to 43C in Seville, 42C in Córdoba and Jaén, and 40C in Cádiz, Granada and Huelva.
On Friday, the extreme heat will spread into northern and eastern Spain, while easing in parts of the south - although temperatures are still forecast to reach 42C in Córdoba, 41C in Seville and 40C in Jaén.
Parts of Ciudad Real, Cáceres and Badajoz are also expected to hit 40C, while Barcelona, Toledo, Huesca, Zaragoza, Ávila, Lleida, Tarragona, Navarra and La Rioja could see highs of 39C.
Meanwhile, parts of Madrid, Valencia, Castilla y León, Castilla-La Mancha and Extremadura are likely to see temperatures between 37C and 38C.
AEMET said the heat could continue for several more days beyond Friday, although temperatures are expected to gradually ease.
According to the weather service, the arrival of a DANA - a Spanish acronym for an isolated high-altitude depression - over the south-west of the Iberian Peninsula will draw a mass of warm, dry air carrying suspended dust across much of mainland Spain and the Balearic Islands.
Combined with high levels of sunshine, this will drive temperatures to "very high levels for the time of year", the Public Protection service warned.
So far this year, Spain has recorded 5,232 heat-related deaths - the highest figure since the Daily Mortality Monitoring (MoMo) system began keeping records in 2015.
In August alone, 2,147 deaths were attributed to high temperatures, according to provisional data available on Monday.
This year's figure has already surpassed the previous annual record, set in 2022, when 4,789 heat-related deaths were recorded.
The average temperature in mainland Spain between June 1 and August 31 was 26C - 2.5C above the 1991-2020 average, Spanish public broadcaster RTVE reported on Monday, citing AEMET data.
At the end of last month, AEMET said it was "virtually certain" that 2026 will have been the hottest summer on record in mainland Spain.
It comes after a Met Office report published in May found that there is an 86 per cent chance that at least one year between 2026 and 2030 will be hotter than 2024, currently the planet's warmest year on record.
It also found that there is a 91 per cent chance that global temperatures will temporarily exceed 1.5C above pre-industrial levels in at least one of the next five years.
If global warming exceeds 1.5C - the target limit set by the Paris Agreement - the risk of severe climate impacts rises sharply. These include ecosystem damage, species extinction, more extreme weather, food and water insecurity, heat-related deaths and the loss of ancient ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica, which would cause sea levels to rise dramatically.
